bio.en: Zoelle Egner was one of the earliest employees at Airtable (leading early marketing and customer success), later advised dozens of startups, and is now head of marketing and growth at Block Party.
bio.zh: Zoelle Egner 是 Airtable 最早的员工之一（领导早期营销与客户成功团队），后来为数十家初创公司提供顾问服务，如今是 Block Party 的营销与增长负责人。

summary.en: Zoelle shares lessons from Airtable's earliest days, including how the team broke into tech, built a marketing machine, and used templates and billboards to drive bottom-up growth. She discusses the power of storytelling, why customer success and marketing should be one team, and tactics for punching above your weight as a small startup. The episode is a rich, operator's guide to early-stage marketing and growth.
summary.zh: Zoelle 分享了 Airtable 最早时期的经验，包括团队如何打入科技圈、打造营销机器，以及用模板和广告牌驱动自下而上的增长。她讨论了讲故事的力量、为何客户成功与营销应当合为同一支团队，以及小初创公司“以小博大”的战术。本期是一份丰富的、关于早期营销与增长的运营者指南。

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: There is sometimes a recommendation or an instinct just like, "Ship things super, super quickly and get them out there." And I'm not saying don't move fast. Obviously you need to move fast in the early days, but make sure someone rereads your email so that it sounds good. Invest in having a decent photo or a decent illustration. If you have sample content, this is actually a big one, sample content for your productivity app as an example. Take the time to not have it be like Jane Doe 12 times in the name list. Have it be references to your industry so that people are like, "Oh, hey. That's a joke about Steve Jobs. I'm a designer. This person is thinking about me." (00:00:35): It's small stuff, but it tells that person, like, "The people who worked on this were thinking about me as a customer, they built it with me in mind, and that means that it is more likely that this is going to fit my needs than something generic." And that builds up both the brand trust that we've talked about, but also the personality of the company, and makes people want to root for you. And frankly, when you are small, you need everyone rooting for you that you can possibly get.
turns.zh: 有时候会有这样一种建议或本能反应，比如“超级、超级快速地把东西做出来，推出去就好”。我并不是说不要快速行动。早期你显然需要快速推进，但一定要确保有人把你的邮件再读一遍，让它听起来得体。在有一张像样的照片或插画上花点心思。如果你有示例内容——这一点其实很关键，比如你那款生产力应用的示例内容——花点时间别让姓名列表里出现十二次“Jane Doe”这种占位名。换成与你所在行业相关的引用，让人们觉得“哦，嘿，这是个关于 Steve Jobs 的梗。我是设计师，这个人是在想着我。” (00:00:35)：这些都是小事，但它告诉那个人：“做这个产品的人是把我当客户在想的，他们是想着我来打造的，这意味着它比我随便做的通用产品更可能契合我的需求。”而这既积累我们聊过的品牌信任，也塑造了公司的个性，让人们愿意为你加油。说真的，当你还很弱小的时候，你需要每一个能争取到的人为你加油。

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: I am super excited to chat.
turns.zh: 我超级兴奋能聊这个。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Awesome. You're probably best known for your time at Airtable, which, correct me if I'm wrong, you're employee number 11.
turns.zh: 太棒了。你大概最出名的是在 Airtable 的那段经历，如果我没记错的话，你是第 11 号员工？

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: That's right.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, and at Airtable you led marketing, you led the customer success teams, so we're going to chat about all that stuff. But before we get into that, I want to chat briefly about this other project that you worked on, that from the outside felt like a really fascinating thing, and a really impactful project, and a really cool team. And it's called Vaccinate California, I think, is that how you pronounce it?
turns.zh: 好的，在 Airtable 你领导了营销，也领导了客户成功团队，所以这些我们都会聊。但在那之前，我想先简单聊聊你参与的另一个项目，从外面看它非常吸引人、影响力很大、团队也很酷。它叫 Vaccinate California，我想——是这么念吗？

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: Mm-hmm.
turns.zh: 嗯哼。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: See, I just-
turns.zh: 看，我刚——

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: VaccinateCA.
turns.zh: VaccinateCA。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: VaccinateCA. Okay. Could you just talk a little bit about what this was? What were you trying to do? What was the impact you had? How did it all go?
turns.zh: VaccinateCA。好的。你能稍微讲讲这到底是什么吗？你们当时想做什么？带来了什么影响？整个过程是怎样的？

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: Yeah, absolutely. So VaccinateCA existed to help people in California find and get a COVID vaccine as quickly as possible, and that sounds really trivial right now, but you have to wind back to January of 2020, when vaccines were first coming out, and it was really hard. So just as a reminder, because most of us have blocked that from our memory.
turns.zh: 当然可以。VaccinateCA 存在的意义，就是帮助加州的人尽可能快地找到并打到 COVID 疫苗，这现在听起来好像微不足道，但你得回到 2020 年 1 月，那时候疫苗刚出来，真的特别难。先提醒一下，因为我们大多数人已经把那段记忆屏蔽了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: The federal and state systems didn't really exist yet, and so everything was this horrible hodgepodge, where eligibility depended on not only what state you were in, it was down to the county, and even sometimes the individual facility. You would be at a Walgreens, and talk to them, and they'd be like, "Oh, you have to be over 65, and also in one of these 12 categories of employment in order to get the vaccine." And then you'd go a mile away and they would tell you something totally different. So people would stand in line for hours. There were phones going off the hook, utterly madness, and really, really scary for a lot of people who were trying to figure out how to keep themselves safe.
turns.zh: 当时联邦和各州的系统都还没真正建立起来，所以一切都乱成一团，资格要求不仅取决于你在哪个州，还精确到县，有时甚至精确到具体接种点。你在 Walgreens 跟他们聊，他们会说“哦，你得满 65 岁，而且得属于这 12 类职业之一才能打疫苗”。结果你走一英里到另一个地方，他们告诉你的又完全不一样。所以人们要排几个小时的队。电话被打爆，简直一团乱麻，对很多想要搞清楚怎么保护自己的安全的人来说，真的非常吓人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I remember those days well.
turns.zh: 是啊，那段日子我记得很清楚。

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: Yeah. So this organization was founded essentially by a tweet by Patrick McKenzie, for those of you who are on Hacker News Patio11. And he had basically this really simple premise, which is, "If you call a pharmacist, and you ask them who they can give a vaccine to, and what vaccine they have, and then you put that answer on a map, someone else doesn't have to make the same phone call. And that takes lots of pressure also as a healthcare system and also helps people to match supply and demand." (00:06:47): So surprisingly, somehow, that tweet, which is essentially like, "Call people, put in spreadsheet, put online," turned into an entire, full nonprofit that was mostly on Discord, Zoom, Airtable, and not only had this entire hundreds of volunteers who were making phone calls in the state of California and eventually, actually, nationally, we became Vaccinate The States eventually, we were also doing this thing called web banking. So we would go and scrape all the official sources as they started coming out, and then validate them because they were not always correct. And eventually we had the most comprehensive database and map of locations in the entire country, including more comprehensive than the federal government and most of the states because they had really complicated limitations on what they could and couldn't publish based on some relationships they had. We didn't have those limitations. (00:07:37): So it meant that we became this clearing house, essentially, for this information and we built an API. We were working directly with Google. And if you ever looked up vaccine locations on Google Maps, that was us feeding that to them, which was really cool. And we also made maps you could see on county websites, so it would help you understand what was available in your area. One of the coolest things that I've ever worked on.
turns.zh: 是的。所以这个组织本质上是由 Patrick McKenzie 的一条推文发起的，Hacker News 上的朋友应该知道他叫 Patio11。他的前提非常简单：“如果你给药剂师打个电话，问他们能把疫苗给谁、他们有什么疫苗，然后把答案标在地图上，别人就不用再打同样的电话了。这既能给医疗系统减压，也能帮助人们匹配供需。” (00:06:47)：所以令人意外的是，那条本质上就是“给人打电话、填进表格、发到网上”的推文，竟然变成了一个完整的非营利组织，主要运作在 Discord、Zoom、Airtable 上。我们不仅有了几百名志愿者在加州打电话，后来实际上扩展到了全国——我们最终改名为 Vaccinate The States——我们还做了一种叫 web banking 的事情。我们会去抓取所有开始出现的官方信息源，然后去做核实，因为它们并不总是准确的。最终我们拥有了全美最全面的接种点数据库和地图，比联邦政府和大多数州还要全面，因为他们基于一些关系，对能发布和不能发布的内容有非常复杂的限制。而我们没有这些限制。(00:07:37)：所以我们实质上成了这些信息的交换中心，并且构建了一个 API。我们直接和 Google 合作。如果你曾经在 Google Maps 上查过疫苗接种点，那就是我们把数据喂给他们的，这真的很酷。我们还做了可以显示在县网站上的地图，帮助你了解自己所在区域有哪些接种点。这是我做过的最酷的事情之一。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, exactly. That's exactly I imagined how epic this was. Just to make sure people understand what you're describing, basically you had hundreds of people sitting there on phones calling vaccine locations, getting the specifics of who is able to get a vaccine there, and then just giving people a pointer of where they can get a vaccine.
turns.zh: 对，没错。这跟我想象的一样宏大。为了让大家理解你描述的情形：基本上就是几百个人坐在电话旁，给各个接种点打电话，搞清楚谁能去那里打疫苗的具体信息，然后给人们一个去哪里能打疫苗的指引。

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: Exactly. So I came in initially, a colleague of mine at Airtable had been helping out with the building out of the backend. And they started getting media attention. And they thought, "Oh, well this will help more people understand that this resource is available." So I got brought in to do some PR help, basically help them figure out how to get the word out, and then ended up actually quitting my job at Airtable to work on it full-time.
turns.zh: 没错。我最初是以顾问身份加入的——我在 Airtable 的一位同事一直在帮忙搭建后端。他们开始受到媒体关注。他们想“哦，这能帮助更多人知道有这个资源可用”。所以我就被请来帮忙做 PR，基本上是帮他们想办法把消息传出去，结果后来我真的辞掉了 Airtable 的工作，全职投入其中。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh wow.
turns.zh: 哦，哇。

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: Yeah, I was on the board and also managing all outreach and other stuff. So we did lots of really cool education, helping people understand their eligibility at all. Built a bunch of fun tools for that as well, but it was a pretty incredible six months, where we filled a really critical gap in the infrastructure of the country.
turns.zh: 是的，我当时在董事会，也负责管理所有的对外联络和其他事务。我们做了很多很酷的科普工作，帮助人们搞清楚自己到底有没有资格。还为此开发了一堆有趣的小工具，但那是一段相当不可思议的六个月，我们填补了国家基础设施中一个非常关键的缺口。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's wild that was the best solution, is just call people and create your own.
turns.zh: 最疯狂的是，最好的解决方案居然就是给人打电话，然后自己建一套。

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: You know?
turns.zh: 你懂吧？

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I imagine there was, at Airtable, were you using to store the data?
turns.zh: 我猜——在 Airtable 里，你们是用它来存储数据的吧？

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: Oh yes.
turns.zh: 哦，当然。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: We built an entire insane database, and then eventually custom software on top of that, to make the people who are making the phone calls more easily get the information in. It was a whole thing. Very cool to see, though, not just tech people get involved. We had, in our volunteer base, people from absolutely every walk of life, not just in California, globally. I remember there was a volunteer who said that he decided to join, he was based in Israel, and he had had no trouble getting the vaccine whatsoever, but seen something on Twitter about it, and just decided he wanted to make sure that people were able to get the vaccine as easily as he did. And he spent dozens of hours calling folks, even though he was in a totally different time zone. But really lovely to see all these different people, retired teachers. I think we had a bunch of 12 year olds who were helping out on the code, of all things, all who just really wanted to make sure that they could keep their community safe.
turns.zh: 我们搭建了一整套疯狂的数据库，后来又在这之上做了定制软件，让打电话的人能更轻松地把信息录进去。那是一整套东西。不过最酷的是看到不只是技术圈的人参与进来。我们的志愿者来自各行各业，不只是加州，而是全球各地。我记得有个志愿者说他决定加入时，他住在以色列，自己打疫苗一点都不费劲，但他看了 Twitter 上关于这件事的内容，就决定要让别人也能像他一样轻松地打到疫苗。他花了几十年小时打电话，尽管他处在完全不同的时区。看到这些完全不同的人——退休教师——真的让人感动。我记得还有一群 12 岁的小孩在帮忙写代码，天知道，他们都只是真心想确保自己的社区能安全。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What happened with this organization? It's a nonprofit that now continues to run or what's happening?
turns.zh: 这个组织后来怎么样了？它是一个现在还在运行的非营利机构，还是说发生了什么？

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: No, we did something which is not common. We actually decided to shut it down after six months. Partially, that's because the existing system finally caught up. And frankly we didn't want to be in a place where we were pulling away resources that could be put towards other things that are going to be more impactful. We always saw ourselves as a stop gap, and once we got to the place where we felt like we weren't really being additive, we wanted to get people's time back, so they could work on other things. So it doesn't exist anymore. I think you can still go check out the archive. We found some researchers who are doing interesting research on it, because there's very fascinating data in there about the equitability of some of the distribution of the vaccine based on where it was available, but the organization is gone. We had that beautiful moment in time and have all moved on. Hoping we don't have to get the band back together, because hopefully it's not necessary anymore.
turns.zh: 没有，我们做了一件不常见的事。我们其实决定在六个月后把它关掉了。一部分原因是，现有的系统终于跟了上来。而且坦白说，我们不想陷入这样一种境地：把资源从其他更有影响力的事情上抽走。我们一直把自己看作一个临时补丁，一旦到了我们觉得自己的存在不再真正带来增量的阶段，我们就想把大家的时间还给他们，好让他们去做别的事。所以它现在已经不存在了。我想你还能去查看它的存档。我们找到了一些研究者，正在对它做有趣的研究，因为里面的数据非常迷人，能反映基于接种点分布差异的疫苗公平性，但组织本身已经不在了。我们拥有过那个美好的瞬间，然后都向前走了。希望我们不必再把这支队伍重组起来，因为希望那已经不再必要了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, man. I'm watching The Last of Us right now about this-
turns.zh: 哦老天。我最近正在看《最后生还者》，讲的就是这个——

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: Mushroom people.
turns.zh: 蘑菇人。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... mushroom based disease, and that scares me now.
turns.zh: ……蘑菇引发的传染病，现在这让我有点害怕。

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Anyway, on this podcast I try to get to things people learn from these experiences, and so I have to ask what you learn about forming something like this, just ad hoc, pulling a bunch of people together, and having them focus, and get things done, or just scaling it, or even shutting down. I guess what have you taken away from that experience that you maybe will bring to either future one-off things like this or even just your work in general?
turns.zh: 总之，在这个播客里我总是想挖掘人们从这些经历中学到的东西，所以我必须问：你从组建这样一个东西——临时起意、把一群人聚到一起、让他们聚焦并把事做成，或者把它做大，甚至最后关掉——中学到了什么？我想，你从这段经历中带走了什么，可能会带到未来类似的临时项目里，甚至带到你平时的日常工作中？

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: Yeah, I'd say probably three things. One, the incredible power of a simple idea to bring people together. One of the reasons why VaccinateCA was so powerful and got so many people to help is everybody immediately understood why it would be useful and how they specifically could be making a difference. And combining those two things was an incredible way to bring a lot of people on board very quickly, because from a messaging perspective, messaging, something very important to me as a marketer, it was so concise. Like, "Pick up phone, help save lives." Really straightforward. People really, really got that. It allowed them to feel like they had agency in a time when everything felt really, really out of control. I think there's a lot of opportunities we have to activate our communities and give people that sense of control that are both going to be helpful more broadly for society, but also just for those individuals as well to make them feel a little bit more safe, a little bit more like they can actually have a difference in things. (00:12:34): I think in tech we often don't jump into these problems. This was not sophisticated technology. It was phones, Discord, and Airtable mostly being used like a spreadsheet. It wasn't anything wild. Even that very simple infrastructure was enough to make a huge difference. And we have some evidence that we saved a lot of lives as a result of it, which is pretty special. I think part of it is also just saying, "We don't have to be hesitant to jump into these problems. It's important to engage with experts in the field, is not to say that tech solutionism is always the answer." And again, this is not super sophisticated technology, but because we were able to go in and talk to the people who are actually affected, get into the system that already existed, and make something really simple, really fast, it actually did have a huge difference and that's really exciting.
turns.zh: 嗯，我想大概是三件事。第一，一个简单的想法能把人凝聚起来的惊人力量。VaccinateCA 之所以那么强大、能召集那么多人帮忙，原因之一是所有人都立刻明白了它为什么有用，以及自己具体能做出什么不同。把这两点结合起来，是极其快速地让大量人加入的妙招，因为从信息传递的角度看——作为营销人，这点对我特别重要——它非常简洁。就像“拿起电话，救人性命”。特别直白。人们真的、真的理解它。它让人在一切都感觉完全失控的时候，觉得自己还有能动性。我觉得我们有很多机会去激活我们的社群，给人们那种掌控感，这既对整个社会更广泛地有益，也能让那些个人感觉更安全一点，更觉得自己真的能改变一些事。(00:12:34)：我觉得在科技行业，我们常常不敢跳进这类问题。但这并不是什么高深的技术。就是电话、Discord，以及主要被当表格用的 Airtable。没什么花哨的。但即使这么简单的基础设施，也足以带来巨大的不同。我们有一些证据表明，我们因此拯救了很多生命，这相当特别。我觉得其中一部分也是在说：“我们不必犹豫要不要跳进这些问题。去和领域内的专家合作很重要，但这并不是说技术万能论永远是答案。”再说一次，这不是什么特别高深的技术，但因为我们能走进去、和真正受影响的人交谈、接入已经存在的系统，并且非常快、非常简单地做出点东西，它实际上就带来了巨大不同，这真的很令人兴奋。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just to double-click on that one, actually reminds me, some founders of companies I've invested in, I often hear how much easier it is for companies that have a mission that people are excited about for them to hire versus companies that don't. And so it's a really good reminder of just the power of having a mission and a vision that is really compelling to people versus some B2B software that people aren't [inaudible 00:13:47] excited about, even though there's a great reason to have great B2B software. Love B2Bs.
turns.zh: 就这点我再深入说一下，这其实让我想起，在我投资的一些公司的创始人身上，我经常听到：那些有着让人们兴奋的使命的公司，招人要比没有使命的公司容易得多。所以这是一个很好的提醒——拥有一个真正能打动人的使命和愿景，其力量远远大于一些人们[听不清 00:13:47]并不兴奋的 B2B 软件，尽管优秀的 B2B 软件本身有充分的理由存在。我爱 B2B。

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: There are. I love great B2B software. I've spent most of my career on it. But I agree with you. I think if you have an authentic mission and people aren't just like, "Oh, sure, okay. You're connecting the world." But really it's some telephony startup. Like, "Okay."
turns.zh: 确实。我爱优秀的 B2B 软件。我职业生涯大部分时间都花在这上面。但我同意你说的。我觉得如果你有一个真实的使命，而不是人们只是敷衍说“哦，当然，好啊，你在连接世界”，结果其实是个什么电话创业公司。那种情况，就“嗯，行吧”。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: If people feel like it's genuinely authentic to what you're building, it can be incredibly meaningful.
turns.zh: 如果人们觉得它真的和你正在构建的东西是吻合的、真诚的，那就会极其有意义。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah. I just remember a founder who, he is a second company, because the first company did not have an amazing mission. The second one did. And like, "Wow. So much easier to hire for this new startup."
turns.zh: 嗯。我就记得一个创始人，这是他的第二家公司，因为第一家没有特别棒的使命。第二家有。然后他就说“哇，这家新公司招人轻松太多了”。

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So totally get that.
turns.zh: 所以我完全理解。

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: Absolutely.
turns.zh: 绝对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay, number two and three.
turns.zh: 好的，第二和第三点。

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: Number two and three, I'll try and be more brief.
turns.zh: 第二和第三点，我会尽量简短点。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It's all good.
turns.zh: 没事的。

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: Number two, I would say just the importance of relentlessly repeating the exact same stuff over and over again, even if you feel like everyone definitely knows. This is something that I've seen play out in every single leadership role that I've had, but it was never more acute than here, particularly because we had this broad coalition of hundreds of people with very different backgrounds. Some people coming to the meeting, some people not, whatever else. I think I repeated the same three talking points about why what we were doing mattered 5,000 times. Cannot overemphasize how many times I said the same stuff, and so did every other member of the board. It really is important and people will fill in the blanks with totally wild things if you don't continuously have that discipline of repeating yourself. You just have to get used to saying the same stuff. And if you do it correctly, it's super motivating. Even if you're sitting there being like, oh my gosh, "I have to say it again." it's worth it.
turns.zh: 第二点，我想说的是：不厌其烦地、一遍又一遍地重复完全相同的内容，这种重要性——哪怕你觉得所有人都肯定知道了。这是我在每一个领导岗位上都能看到的现象，但从来没有比在这里更尖锐的，尤其是因为我们有一个由数百名背景截然不同的人组成的广泛联盟。有人来开会，有人不来，诸如此类。我想我把那三条“我们做的事为什么重要”的要点重复了 5000 遍。我怎么强调都不为过，我说了多少遍同样的话，其他每一位董事会成员也是。这真的很重要，如果你不能持续地保持重复自己的纪律，人们就会用完全离谱的东西来填补空白。你就是得习惯说同样的话。而且如果你做得对，它会超级激励人。哪怕你坐在那里心里想“天哪，我又得说一遍”，那也是值得的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: This reminds me, I don't know where I saw this, it's just in my head right now, that the CEO and founder's job, their actual title is repeater in chief.
turns.zh: 这让我想起——我不知道在哪儿看到的，现在就冒出来了——CEO 和创始人的工作，他们真正的头衔应该是“首席复读机”。

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: It absolutely should be.
turns.zh: 它绝对应该是。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: It resonates. Yeah.
turns.zh: 很有共鸣。是的。

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: I've worked with some leaders who never wanted to. They're like, "No, this is going to be boring for people." And you just have to be like, "Honestly, most people are never listening as much as you think that they are."
turns.zh: 我合作过一些领导，他们从来不想这么做。他们会说“不，这会让人们觉得无聊”。但你只能告诉自己“老实说，大多数人根本不像你想的那么认真在听”。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: "We wish that they would. But you have to say it 12 different ways in writing, and out loud, and all this other stuff. You're never as important as you think you are, unfortunately, when it comes to that."
turns.zh: “我们倒是希望他们听。但你得用 12 种不同的方式，写下来、说出来，还有各种其他形式。不幸的是，在这方面你从来不像自己以为的那么重要。”

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Oh, these are great lessons. Okay. What else do you tell?
turns.zh: 哦，这些都是很棒的教训。好的。你还有别的要分享的吗？

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: I think my last learning was really about the power of having a laughably small MVP for something. By the end of this, we were covering the entire United States. We had an API, we had custom software on the front end, this whole behemoth of stuff that we got to in four months or something. In the beginning it was truly, basically, a spreadsheet, and phones, and that was it. Even that, for the first few weeks while we were getting the rest of the infrastructure really going, not only had tremendous impact at one of the most important parts in the pandemic, but also gave us so much information about we actually needed to build that was going to be helpful. And I remember having all of these assumptions about what was going to be necessary to manage this coalition of people to make sure that we had really good data quality. (00:16:41): Because one of the most important things you can do if you're trying to be a trusted source of truth is actually have the correct information. Sounds trivial, it's not at all at that scale. And I was totally wrong about all my assumptions. I thought we were going to have to have totally different types of oversight. I thought we were going to have totally different tooling. And it turned out we could do something way lighter weight that would allow us to move much faster as the regulatory landscape kept changing, as all the rule making at individual places kept changing. And that agility, that willingness to do just the smallest possible thing is obviously a little bit of a trope in the industry. (00:17:15): People talk about it a lot, but it's never been driven home to me so much, because we're talking about something that had incredibly high stakes as people's health, and we're still able to do it in that context. So if we could do it there, you can imagine that the applications of that in other industries are just tremendous. So yeah, if you're listening to this, and you were thinking maybe you needed to add more stuff, I bet you could prune.
turns.zh: 我想我最后一条心得，真的关于拥有一个小到可笑的 MVP 的力量。到这事儿结尾时，我们已经覆盖整个美国。我们有了 API，有了前端的定制软件，这一大堆东西，是我们在四个月左右的时间里长出来的。而一开始，它真的、基本上就是一张表格，加上电话，仅此而已。即便那样，在头几周我们还在搭建其余基础设施的时候，它不但在疫情中最重要的环节之一产生了巨大的影响，还给了我们大量信息，让我们知道到底需要构建什么才有帮助。我还记得我当时有一堆假设，关于要管理好这群人、确保数据质量需要什么。(00:16:41)：因为如果你要想成为可信的信息源，你能做的最重要的事情之一，就是提供正确的信息。听起来简单，在那个规模下根本不简单。而我的所有假设都大错特错。我以为我们需要完全不同类型的监督机制，我以为我们需要完全不同的工具。结果我们发现，可以用轻量得多的方案，让我们在监管环境不断变、各个地方的规则不断改的情况下，移动得快得多。而这种敏捷、这种只做最小可行之事的意愿，显然在行业里有点老生常谈了。(00:17:15)：人们常说，但它从没像这次这样打动我，因为我们在说的是一件利害极其重大、关乎人们健康的事，而我们仍然能在那样的情境下做到。所以如果我们在那种情况下都能做到，你可以想象它在其他行业的应用会有多惊人。所以，如果你在听这期节目，并且你当时在想也许你需要加更多东西，我打赌你其实可以删减。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And it's nice to have the forcing function where the world is changing so quickly and the team's probably small, where you are forced to build small. Which I think is why this reminder is so important. Oftentimes you have more resources, and you end up building more just because you can. And yeah, what you're saying is oftentimes, "It'll shoot you in the foot."
turns.zh: 而且这种“强制函数”很好——世界变化那么快、团队可能很小，你被迫做得很小。我想这就是为什么这个提醒这么重要。很多时候你有更多资源，结果就因为能做，你反而建了更多。而你说得对，很多时候这“会搬起石头砸自己的脚”。

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing. I didn't expect to get into this much detail with VaccinateCA and so I'm glad we did. Let's zoom out a little bit, and just fill in some gaps on your background, briefly. Can you just highlight some of the other wonderful things you've done in career? Airtable, we talked about, VaccinateCA, just broadly, what else have you been up to?
turns.zh: 太棒了。我没料到会和 VaccinateCA 聊这么细，不过我很高兴我们聊了。我们稍微拉远一点，简单补充一下你背景里的空白。你能简要说说职业生涯里其他精彩的事吗？Airtable 我们聊过了，VaccinateCA 也是，总体而言，你还忙些什么？

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: Yeah, absolutely. Okay, so I'll try and be brief. I worked in tech for more than a decade, mostly marketing and customer success, a little bit of ops. Before I got into tech, I was a little bit of a dilettante, so some non-profit, healthcare, dying big box retail, because I graduated right into the recession and I was certain no one would hire me. Turns out that was actually wrong. But on the plus side, now I know what dysfunction looks like at great scale, which is actually quite an education and very useful. But I always knew I wanted to get into tech, partially because I'm from the Bay area, and partially because I had been obsessively power mapping the industry, and looking at its flocking patterns, and who had what types of influence, because I'm a nerd. And I really wanted to see if I could get in, in the first place. Because-
turns.zh: 当然可以。好的，我尽量简短。我在科技行业工作了十多年，主要是营销和客户成功，还有一点运营。在进入科技行业之前，我有点像个半吊子，做过一些非营利组织、医疗、还有濒临倒闭的大卖场零售，因为我毕业时正好赶上经济衰退，我认定没人会雇我。结果证明我错了。但往好处说，现在我见识过大规模失灵长什么样，这其实很有教育意义，也很有用。但我一直都知道我想进科技行业，一部分因为我来自湾区，一部分因为我一直在痴迷地绘制这个行业的权力地图，研究它的集群模式，以及谁拥有什么样的影响力，因为我是个书呆子。而我真的很想看看，自己到底能不能挤进去。因为——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Wait, can you talk about this, which, what is it you did? What did you call, a flocking pattern?
turns.zh: 等等，你能讲讲这个吗——你到底做了什么？你刚才叫它什么，集群模式？

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: Sure. You can imagine in any community, there are nodes of influence, people who know a lot of folks, they have money, whatever it might be. And they're able to direct how that community or that ecosystem evolves. In the tech industry, typically VCs will often play a role in this, but so will certain types of executives. And you can follow how they move between different companies, and who they worked with, and then see that influences who gets investment in the future. It influences the different partnerships that evolve. It influences the assumed wisdom in various different careers. And because I'm a big old nerd, I was literally drawing diagrams based on-
turns.zh: 当然。你可以想象，在任何社群里，都存在影响力的节点——认识很多人、手里有钱、或其他什么的人。他们能够左右那个社群或生态的演化。在科技行业，通常 VC 会在其中扮演重要角色，某些类型的高管也会。你可以追踪他们在不同公司之间怎么流动、和谁共事过，然后就能看出这会影响将来谁拿到投资。它影响演化出的各种合作关系。它影响各行各业里约定俗成的“智慧”。因为我是个老书呆子，我真的会基于——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Whoa.
turns.zh: 哇。

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: ... reading people's blog posts of who was influential in what way? Because I was non-technical. I tried programming, and I hated it, frankly. And so I was like, "Okay, it's 2010, it's 2011. There's not clear ways to get into the industry as a non-technical person. I need to figure out how to do this with people. Because otherwise I'm not sure why someone would take a chance on me with what I have done historically. And that sounds a little insane, but it's very effective. And I ended up getting my start in tech basically by identifying a company where I thought I had a unique set of connections or understanding of the space that they were working in, where I thought I could maybe email the CEO and be helpful.
turns.zh: ……读人们的博客，看谁以什么方式发挥了影响力？因为我不是技术出身。我试过编程，坦白说我很讨厌它。所以我就想“好吧，2010 年、2011 年，作为一个非技术背景的人，没有明确的方式进入这个行业。我得想办法靠人来解决。否则我真不知道凭我过去的那点经历，谁会愿意在我身上赌一把。”这听起来有点疯狂，但非常有效。我最终进入科技行业的方式，基本上就是找到一家我认为自己拥有独特人脉、或对他们所在领域有独特理解的公司，觉得也许我给 CEO 发封邮件就能帮上忙。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: And did this connect to that diagram you drew? Did this help you point in that direction?
turns.zh: 那这和你画的图有关系吗？是它帮你指向了那个方向的吗？

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: Yeah, absolutely. So I was closely tracking YCombinator and that whole ecosystem. So I knew I wanted to find a smaller company, where they maybe were having more difficulty hiring, because they were less well known or a little bit less, I don't know, sexy. But while they were still connected into that broader group, because it has with a pedigree that people would take you seriously if you had worked at a YC backed startup.
turns.zh: 是的，绝对有关。我当时在紧密追踪 YCombinator 和整个生态。所以我知道我想找一家较小的公司，它们可能招人更难一些，因为名气小、或者没那么——我不知道怎么说——性感。但它们仍然连接在更大的圈子里的，因为只要你在一家 YC 投资的创业公司工作过，就有那种血统，人们会认真看待你。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: Anyway, I got really pointy hat strategic about this, but it was effective.
turns.zh: 总之，我在这件事上搞得非常“尖顶帽”式地策略化，但确实有效。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Do you still-
turns.zh: 你现在还——

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: And-
turns.zh: 而且——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: ... have this diagram, by the way? It'd be so funny to look at it right now.
turns.zh: ……还留着这张图吗？现在要是能看一眼会特别好笑。

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: No, I don't think I have it anymore. I might be able to dig it up, but alas, I think it may have been lost in one of my many moves since then.
turns.zh: 不，我想我不再有它了。我也许能把它翻出来，但唉，我想它大概在我后来那么多次搬家中的某一次弄丢了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: All right.
turns.zh: 好的。

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: It's been-
turns.zh: 已经——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: No problem.
turns.zh: 没关系。

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: ... more than a decade.
turns.zh: ……超过十年了。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Okay. I imagine that was true. Okay, so I think I cut you off. You were talking about some of the things you've done in your career.
turns.zh: 好的。我想那倒是真的。好吧，我好像打断你了。你刚才在讲你职业生涯里做过的一些事。

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: Yeah, ended up using my studies of the space to get into a role as employee one at a developer focus YC backed startup. And the funny story on that is that I got that role by cold emailing the CEO while I was still in college. And then he actually followed up with me almost immediately, because I'd offered to introduce him to some professors, which was useful for the type of business. And then I ignored him for two years because I got busy with my thesis, and got other jobs, and whatever, came back to it and wrote this ridiculous apology email, being like, "I promise I respond to emails faster. I see that you're hiring. Would you give me a second chance? Please, can I come work for you? I have no experience that's useful, but I work really hard." And I figured he would either laugh me off of the internet or give me a job, and very fortunately for me, he gave me a job. So thanks, Ryan. Appreciate that. That was how I got into tech.
turns.zh: 对，最后我利用自己对这个领域的钻研，进了一家以开发者为核心、YC 投资的初创公司，成了第 1 号员工。这里有个好笑的故事：我还在上大学的时候就靠冷邮件联系上了他们的 CEO，拿到了这个职位。他几乎立刻就回了我，因为我当时提出可以帮他引荐一些教授，这对那种类型的业务很有用。然后我把他晾了两年，因为我忙着写论文、找了别的工作，反正后来才回过头来，写了封荒唐的道歉邮件，大意是“我保证以后回邮件快多了。我看到你们在招人。能给我个机会吗？求你了，我能来给你干活吗？我没什么有用的经验，但我真的特别努力。”我猜他要么在网上把我当笑话笑掉，要么就给我个 offer，而我很幸运，他给了我一份工作。所以谢谢你，Ryan。我很感激。我就是这么进入科技行业的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Thanks, Ryan.
turns.zh: 谢谢你，Ryan。

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: Yes, we appreciate it. So that startup got acquired by Box. And when I went over to Box, they had never had paying developers before. So we were bringing over seven figure contracts. So I started developer success programs there. And then in a totally wild shift, I ended up moving over to run their social media editorial and internal comms, which doesn't sound related to developer success, but I had always been a writer, and I wrote this blog post about what it was like to be an early stage non-technical employee. There was a little spicy, talking about some of the challenges, and I didn't tell anyone I was going to do it. And I got this email from PR being like, "We need to have a meeting." And I was like, "Oh, they're going to fire me. I went too far." I thought I was being circumspect, that I went too far. And in the meeting they were like, "Hey, we really think you should apply for this job. We would love to have you run social media." Which is not the outcome I expected.
turns.zh: 是的，我们都很感激。那家初创公司后来被 Box 收购了。我转到 Box 的时候，他们以前从来没有过付费的开发者。所以我们是把七位数的合同带过去的。于是我在那里启动了开发者成功项目。然后一个完全意想不到的转折是，我最后转去负责他们的社交媒体编辑和内部沟通——这听起来跟开发者成功不沾边，但我一直是个写作者，我当时写了一篇博客，讲作为一个早期非技术员工是什么滋味。里面有点犀利，谈到了一些挑战，而且我没告诉任何人我要发。然后我收到 PR 部门的一封邮件说“我们需要开个会”。我当时想“哦，他们要炒我了。我太过了。”我以为自己已经够谨慎了，结果还是太过了。结果会上他们却说“嘿，我们真的觉得你应该申请这个岗位。我们很希望由你来负责社交媒体。”这完全不是我预期的结果。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That's a cool learning, there. Just like, "Do stuff." You know? "Don't be afraid."
turns.zh: 这倒是个很酷的领悟。就像——“去干就完了”。你懂吧？“别怕。”

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: Yeah, it was definitely not the expected outcome, but one that was very exciting. So got to go run those programs for a couple years through the IPO, which is a whole education in and of itself, to see how comms changes when you become a public company. And then I was on Hacker News obsessively at the time, and I saw the beta for Airtable come out. Immediately signed up, and became obsessed with the product, and evangelizing it to everybody that I knew and ultimately ended up figuring out a way to finagle my way into that role as employee 11 there. (00:23:43): And it sounds like we're going to talk about Airtable more, so I won't belabor that, but marketing and customer success stuff, ended up leaving for VaccinateCA, and then the last little bit here is just when that ended, I really thought I wanted to start my own company. So I gave myself a certain window in which to try out different ideas, and at the same time was advising and consulting. Ultimately didn't end up finding anything that I felt so much conviction that it was worth blowing up absolutely everything else about my life in order to go heads down on a company. So eventually decided to go in-house with one of the companies I've been advising, Block Party, and now I run marketing and growth there.
turns.zh: 对，这绝对不是预期的结果，但是个让人很兴奋的结果。所以我有机会在 IPO 之前的那几年运营那些项目，这本身就很长见识——你能看到成为上市公司后，沟通方式会发生怎样的变化。那时候我痴迷地刷 Hacker News，看到了 Airtable 的 beta 版发布。我立刻注册了，然后对这个产品欲罢不能，向我认识的每一个人都安利它，最终还想办法绕了进去，成了那里的第 11 号员工。(00:23:43)：听起来我们后面还会更多聊 Airtable，所以这块我就不啰嗦了，但就是营销和客户成功那块，后来我离开去了 VaccinateCA，然后这里最后一点是：当那件事结束后，我真的以为自己想开家公司。所以我给自己定了一个时间窗口去尝试不同的想法，同时也在做顾问和咨询。最终我没找到任何让我有那么强信念、值得为了它把生活里其他一切都掀翻、然后埋头做公司的东西。所以最后我决定加入我一直在顾问的一家公司的内部，也就是 Block Party，现在我在那里负责营销和增长。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Can you just explain Block Party briefly? [inaudible 00:24:21]-
turns.zh: 你能简单介绍一下 Block Party 吗？[听不清 00:24:21]——

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: Absolutely. We're an online safety company. We help users have more control over their digital experience. And our first product is anti-harassment and anti-spam tools for Twitter.
turns.zh: 当然。我们是一家在线安全公司。我们帮助用户更好地掌控自己的数字体验。我们的第一个产品，是针对 Twitter 的反骚扰和反垃圾工具。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: So you've worked at Box, Airtable, now Block Party. You've advised a lot of companies around marketing product growth. I'm curious if there's a thread that has maintained through all of those experiences in terms of what works well for marketing, and growth, and things you've learned that just consistently- [inaudible 00:24:52]
turns.zh: 所以你在 Box、Airtable 工作过，现在是 Block Party。你也给很多公司做过营销、产品、增长方面的顾问。我很好奇，在所有这些经历中，有没有一条贯穿始终的线——关于什么对营销和增长有效、以及你学到的那些始终——[听不清 00:24:52]

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: A few pieces that go into how I choose companies that create that thread. And part of this is about me wanting to match what I think I'm really good at with what will have the greatest leverage for a company that I work at. I've mentioned I'm a writer, really care about telling stories, and helping people to understand new or novel things. I also really care about product quality. I'm a little bit of a product snob. And one of my strengths is enthusiasm. So if I can't genuinely go to a customer and tell them, "This product is going to solve a real problem for you and it's going to be amazing." I can't do my job. So all of the companies that I've chosen to go to have had this foundation of an incredible product experience that maybe people didn't fully understand, and where I could come in and help connect the dots between that amazing product that's going to be really, really helpful and the opportunities for a much wider range of people to benefit from that. (00:25:46): So in practice, what that means is I often end up working at companies that are in a position to really punch above their weight from a brand perspective. They're typically much lower headcount than you would ever expect. They're typically way earlier stage than you would expect, but I've been able to put together a brand or an experience that allows people to invest themselves into the company with a high level of trust, I guess. (00:26:13): I'll be more specific because that's really ambiguous. Airtable, it manages mission critical workflows, highly sensitive data. It's super important. You only use tools you can trust for that type of thing. The same thing is true at Block Party, online safety. You have to trust the company that you're entrusting your safety to. And in my experience, people, and especially founders really underestimate how much every single touchpoint a customer has from word of mouth or the ad that brings them in the door, landing pages, signup flows, customer service experiences. Every single one of those moments is building a brand that is adding or removing trust. (00:26:48): So for me in the early days, that means thinking about like, "What are the signals that I can provide to future customers that say, 'We understand you specifically, and our solution is designed for a person like you.' And two, that will say, 'Hey, we're actually operating on a much higher level than you might expect for a company of our size or our stage. We take this really seriously. We have all the things in place to take care of you. So you shouldn't be afraid to spend six figures or put your safety in our hands because we've got your back. We're doing this the right way.'" Has tremendous dividends when you're in a business that is often driven by word of mouth. Because if you take care of people and you follow up that brand experience with a product experience that is really powerful and actually does the things that says it's going to do, then your word of mouth can become a huge driver of growth for the company. (00:27:40): Of course, the outcome of this in practice is really funny. So I remember really distinctly having to invite customers to go out to lunch with us when they would come to San Francisco back in the Airtable days, because we had 15 people in a teeny tiny office. It's not that I wanted to mislead anyone, but I didn't need to reinforce the fact that they were spending six figures with us when we had 15 people. If they had gone to look on LinkedIn, they could have figured that out, but we didn't need to remind them that we were so small, and they were running some of their most important processes with our product. I think I was on the phone with Slack at one point. And they were like, "Oh, well you guys are probably about the same size company as we are, right?" And I was like, "Not quite. A little smaller, just an entire order of magnitude, no big deal, it's totally fine. We're all smooth. We'll take care of you. It's going to great." But it-
turns.zh: 我选择公司时之所以会形成那条线，有几个要素。其中一部分是我想把我自认为真正擅长的东西，和我所在公司能获得最大杠杆的点匹配起来。我说过我是个写作者，真的很在乎讲故事，帮人们理解新奇的事物。我也真的很在乎产品质量。我有点像个产品势利眼。我的强项之一是热情。所以如果我没有办法真心实意地走到客户面前告诉他们“这个产品会帮你解决一个真实的问题，而且会非常棒”，那我就没法做好我的工作。所以所有我选择去的公司，都有一个基础：一种也许人们还没完全理解、但极为出色的产品体验，而我能够进去，帮他们把“这个会非常、非常有帮助的好产品”和“让更广泛的人群从中受益的机会”连接起来。(00:25:46)：所以实际上，这意味着我经常最后会在那些从品牌角度看，真的能“以小博大”的公司工作。它们的人员规模通常比你想象的少得多，阶段通常比你预期的早得多，但我能够搭建起一个品牌或一种体验，让人们带着高度的信任把自己“投”进这家公司。(00:26:13)：我说得更具体一点，因为刚才说得太模糊了。Airtable 管理的是关键业务流程和高度敏感的数据。这超级重要。这种事你只会用你信得过的工具。Block Party 也是一样，在线安全。你必须信任那家被你托付安全问题的公司。而根据我的经验，人们——尤其是创始人——真的低估了客户经历的每一个触点：无论是口碑、还是把他们带进门的那条广告、落地页、注册流程、客服体验。每一个瞬间都在构建一个增加或削减信任的品牌。(00:26:48)：所以对我来说，在早期，这意味着要去想：“我能给未来的客户传递什么信号，让他们觉得‘我们特别懂你，我们的方案就是为像你这样的人设计的’？第二，让他们觉得‘嘿，我们实际运作的水准，比你们按我们公司规模或阶段预期的要高得多。我们非常认真。我们已经把照顾好你的一切都安排好了。所以你不必害怕花六位数、或者把你的安全交到我们手里，因为我们在挺你。我们是在用正确的方式做这件事。’”当你做的生意常常靠口碑驱动时，这会有巨大的回报。因为如果你照顾好人们，并且用一个真正强大、说到做到的产品体验去接续那个品牌体验，那么你的口碑就会成为公司增长的一大驱动力。(00:27:40)：当然，这事在实践中的结果真的很好笑。我特别清楚地记得，在 Airtable 早期，当有客户来旧金山时，我们得邀请他们和我们出去吃午饭，因为当时我们只有 15 个人，挤在一个极小的办公室里。倒不是我想误导谁，而是我不需要去强化“他们正和一家只有 15 人的公司做着六位数的生意”这个事实。如果他们去 LinkedIn 上看，他们也能发现，但我们没必要提醒他们我们这么小、而他们却用我们的产品在跑一些最重要的流程。我记得有一次和 Slack 通电话。他们说“哦，你们大概和我们公司规模差不多，对吧？”我说“不完全是。小一点，就整整差一个数量级，没什么大不了的，完全没问题。我们一切顺利。我们会照顾好你的。会很棒的。”但是——

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Amazing.
turns.zh: 太棒了。

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: ... really makes a difference, all of those little things.
turns.zh: ……所有这些小事，真的会带来不同。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: That reminds me, I heard stories of very early Airbnb days where they had to take meetings in a bathroom, or in the hallway, and they did interviews, I think in the hallway because there was no space.
turns.zh: 这让我想起，我听过 Airbnb 很早期的故事，他们不得不在洗手间里开会，或者在走廊里，我想他们连面试都是在走廊里做的，因为没地方。

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: We did a lot of calling from the hallway at Airtable, also from this weird internal patio you could only get to through climbing through a window. The window kept breaking. And so I, at one point, remember someone getting stuck outside trying to interview someone with the windows closed. Utter, utter ridiculous nonsense. But you know, that's all the fun things that happened in the early days before you become bigger.
turns.zh: 我们在 Airtable 也常在走廊里打电话，还有从一个奇怪的内部天井打，那个天井只能爬窗才能进去。窗户老坏。所以我有一次记得，有人试图面试别人时，窗户关上了，结果被卡在了外面。彻头彻尾的荒唐事。但你知道，这些都是你在变大之前早期日子里发生的有趣事。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Yeah, I love those early day stories.
turns.zh: 是啊，我爱听那些早期的故事。

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 嗯。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I really love the concept of punching above your weight as a startup. What else did you do at Air Table or other places that help you do that? One is just don't let them see how small you are, necessarily. Are there any other technical things you recall that like, "Oh, here's things that really worked really well for punching above our weight as a small company at that point."
turns.zh: 我真的很喜欢“初创公司以小博大”这个概念。你在 Airtable 或其他地方还做了什么来帮助实现这一点？其中之一就是不一定要让他们看到你有多小。你还记得其他什么具体管用的招数吗——比如“哦，这些招在那时作为一家小公司真的特别好用地帮我们以小博大”？

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: A couple of these things are very unsexy, but very useful. One, make sure that your landing pages, and your emails, and other things have a level of polish that makes them feel a little bit more done. I think there is sometimes a recommendation or an instinct just like, "Ship things super, super quickly and get them out there." And I'm not saying don't move fast. Obviously you need to move fast in the early days, but make sure someone rereads your email so that it sounds good. Invest in having a decent photo or a decent illustration. If you have sample content, this is actually a big one, sample content for your productivity app as an example. Take the time to not have it be like Jane Doe 12 times in the name list. Have it be references to your industry so that people are like, "Oh, hey. That's a joke about Steve Jobs. I'm a designer. This person is thinking about me." (00:30:20): It's small stuff, but it tells that person, like, "The people who worked on this were thinking about me as a customer, they built it with me in mind, and that means that it is more likely that this is going to fit my needs than something generic." And that builds up both the brand trust that we've talked about, but also the personality of the company, and makes people want to root for you. And frankly, when you are small, you need everyone rooting for you that you can possibly get. (00:30:45): So those little bits of polish that don't take a ton of time are absolutely worth it. The last thing I would say is making sure that in your public communications launches, if you ever talk to press, which some companies can and some companies can't, having more of a point of view than just about your product, you can try and say, like, "We are part of something bigger. Here's the broader circle or movement that we are a part of." It makes it feel more inevitable and more like you're not just self servingly talking about your tiny corner of the world, but that it's actually part of this much bigger trend. It will be more compelling and it feels like you're operating at a different level of sophistication that can be really helpful.
turns.zh: 有几件事非常不性感，但非常有用。第一，确保你的落地页、邮件以及其他东西，有一种完成度，让人感觉稍微更“做完了”。我觉得有时候会有一种建议或本能，比如“超级、超级快地把东西做出来推出去”。我并不是说不要快。早期你显然需要快，但一定要确保有人把你的邮件再读一遍，让它听起来得体。在有一张像样的照片或插画上花点心思。如果你有示例内容——这一点其实很关键，比如你那款生产力应用的示例内容——花点时间别让姓名列表里出现十二次“Jane Doe”。换成与你所在行业相关的引用，让人们觉得“哦，嘿，这是个关于 Steve Jobs 的梗。我是设计师，这个人是在想着我。”(00:30:20)：这些都是小事，但它告诉那个人：“做这个产品的人是把我当客户在想的，他们是想着我来打造的，这意味着它比我随便做的通用产品更可能契合我的需求。”而这既积累我们聊过的品牌信任，也塑造了公司的个性，让人们愿意为你加油。说真的，当你还很弱小的时候，你需要每一个能争取到的人为你加油。(00:30:45)：所以那些不花太多时间的微小打磨，绝对值得。我要说的最后一点是：在你的对外沟通、发布活动中，如果你会跟媒体打交道——有些公司能、有些不能——确保你的“观点”不只关于你的产品本身，你可以试着说“我们是一个更宏大事物的一部分。这是我们所属的更广阔的圈子或运动”。这会让它感觉更势不可挡，也更像你不只是在自私地谈论自己那小小的一亩三分地，而是它真的是一个更大趋势的一部分。这会更有说服力，而且会让人觉得你运作在另一种更老练的水准上，这真的很有帮助。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I love that. On the first point, basically, it's attention to detail and obsession with quality is what I'm hearing.
turns.zh: 我喜欢这点。关于第一点，我听到的核心其实就是注重细节、对质量的痴迷。

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: Yes.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: Just to make it clear, this isn't just a tiny team just pushing the stuff out. I imagine most founders would be like, "Yes, I would love, we are going to focus on quality. We'll make sure everything looks great." In reality it always is this trade off against other things they could be doing.
turns.zh: 我要说清楚，这不只是一个小团队把东西推出去那么简单。我想大多数创始人都会说“是的，我们很愿意、我们会专注质量。我们会确保一切都看起来很棒”。但现实中，这总是和他们本可以做的其他事之间的权衡。

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: Yep.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What do you think folks can do to help keep that level of quality high? Is it just one person being obsessed and just reviewing everything like a founder? Is having someone like you that's just very detail oriented, just review everything? How do you actually execute that when you have 1,000 things to do?
turns.zh: 你觉得大家能做些什么来维持这种高质量的水准？是只需要一个人像创始人那样痴迷、审阅一切吗？还是说有个像你这样非常注重细节的人来审阅一切？当你有一千件事要做的时候，你到底怎么执行这件事？

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: 100%. I'd say there's one of two approaches and you articulated them here. One is you can have the founder that is the avatar of quality, who is just relentlessly being like, "Hey, we're going to do the 15 minute check. Yes, we're going through it. Yes, I'm going to send you a copy of this email, and someone else going to click every link in it, and make sure they're not broken." Or, you can have someone else be the avatar of that who is in the company. I would say in many of the companies I have worked at, that has been me, because I've been the marketing human who cares. But it doesn't have to be a marketing person, it can be someone on product. It can be, honestly, even someone on customer success if you're willing to let them provide their feedback on the way that you're showing up in the world, which you should because they have fantastic insight. There just needs to be someone. (00:32:50): And I think building that into how you interview can be very helpful, as well. So finding people who understand those trade-offs and that balance, and who are willing to put in the extra 15 minutes, but aren't going to spend an extra week trying to obsessively QA everything. You don't want to go that far. Just who has that bent towards detail can be very helpful. Also, just make yourself a checklist. It doesn't have to be complicated. "Every time we put out a blog post, these are the three things we're going to do. Every time we send out an email, it needs to be seen by at least one other person." None of this is rocket science. You just need to make a little process for yourself, and then it can be very fast and lightweight, but the dividends are worth it, I think.
turns.zh: 百分之百。我想有两种路径，你也说到了。一种是让创始人成为“质量化身”， relentless 地像个监督员：“嘿，我们要做那个 15 分钟检查。对，我们在走流程。对，我会把邮件副本发给你，然后另一个人去点里面的每一个链接，确保没坏。”或者，你也可以让公司里的另一个人来做这个质量化身。我想在我工作过的很多公司里，那个人就是我，因为我是那个在乎的营销人。但它不一定是营销的人，可以是产品的人。老实说，甚至可以是客户成功的人——只要你愿意让他们就“你对外呈现的方式”提供反馈，而你应该这么做，因为他们有极棒的洞察。关键在于总得有个人。(00:32:50)：而且我觉得把这纳入你的招聘方式也很有帮助。所以要找那些理解这些权衡和平衡、愿意多花那 15 分钟、但又不会多花一整周去 obsessive 地 QA 一切的人。你不想走到那一步。只要找有那种细节倾向的人就很有帮助。另外，就给自己做个清单。不必复杂。“每次我们发博客，这三件事要做。每次我们发邮件，至少要另一个人看过。”这些都不是什么高深学问。你只需要为自己建立一点流程，它就可以非常快、非常轻量，但回报是值得的，我想。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: I like how simple this is, just to look like a bigger company, is just pay attention and focus on the little things. It's not a big, whole thing. [inaudible 00:33:39]
turns.zh: 我喜欢这有多简单——要想看起来像家更大的公司，就是多上心、专注在小事上。它不是什么大工程。[听不清 00:33:39]

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: There are some bigger things you can do if you really need to. My favorite silly example of this is Airtable, back in the day, got roasted on Twitter for having billboards that were not super specific about a specific problem or whatever. They were just billboards that we had out. And everyone was like, "This makes no sense. Why are you doing this? We don't understand." They were actually super effective for us because we had a different goal than everyone thought that we did. (00:34:03): For us, it was all about signaling to some very large companies that we were a legitimate and large enough company that they could trust, and we had geographical concentration in specific areas, because we were in the fashion industry, the media industry in New York, we knew exactly where all of their offices were and we knew if they saw our billboards, walking to work, and then got the request to IT for the budget in order to pay six figures for Airtable, they were more likely to be like, "Oh, it's not just some weird startup we never heard of." Like, "Oh, I've seen that billboard, they must be legitimate." And that sounds really silly, but it wasn't actually that expensive. (00:34:40): We got mostly remnant inventory, which is at the end of a particular buying cycle. Sometimes they haven't fully sold everything, and you can get the slightly less good ones that are still maybe where you want them for really cheap. And everyone thinks that you only buy billboards if you're huge. So that small signaling thing was a way for us to make sure that we remove some of the risk of not being able to close deals because we were so small. So you can get creative about it. Most of the time you're not going to do that. Most of the time it's like, "Reread your emails." But you could also push it even further if you need to.
turns.zh: 如果你真的需要，也有一些更大的动作可以做。我最喜欢的一个傻例子是，早年的 Airtable 因为在 Twitter 上投放那些没有特别针对某个具体问题的广告牌而被群嘲。那些就是我们立在那里的广告牌。大家都说“这完全没道理。你们为什么要这么做？我们看不懂。”但它们对我们来说其实超级有效，因为我们的目标和大家以为的不一样。(00:34:03)：对我们来说，这完全是为了向一些非常大的公司释放信号：我们是一家合法、而且足够大的、他们可以信任的公司，而且我们在特定区域有地理上的集中——因为我们在时尚行业、纽约的媒体行业，我们确切知道他们所有的办公室在哪，我们知道如果他们在上班路上看到我们的广告牌，然后向 IT 申请预算来为 Airtable 支付六位数，他们更可能会想“哦，这不只是某家我们从来没听过怪 startup”。而是“哦，我见过那个广告牌，他们肯定是正规的”。这听起来真的很傻，但其实没那么贵。(00:34:40)：我们拿到的多数是 remnant inventory（剩余的库存位），也就是某个购买周期末尾剩下的。有时候他们没完全卖光，你就能以极便宜的价格拿到那些稍微差一点、但位置可能仍然正是你要的地方。而所有人都以为只有大公司才会买广告牌。所以那个小小的信号动作，是我们用来消除“因为太小而没法成交”这种风险的一种方式。所以你可以很有创意地去做。大多数时候你不会去做那个。大多数时候就是“把邮件再读一遍”。但如果你需要，也可以推得更远。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: What is that full rough cost of billboards like? Because I think people think about billboards and it's hard to even know what they cost. What's a number?
turns.zh: 那广告牌整体大概要花多少钱？因为我觉得人们想到广告牌时，连它们要花多少钱都很难有个概念。能给个数吗？

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: It really, really depends, so I'm hesitant to give you a number because which metro you're in, it ranges vastly. I would say you can expect that some of that inventory is in the low thousands of dollars, which is way lower than you might expect.
turns.zh: 这真的、真的因情况而异，所以我不太想给你一个具体数字，因为你所在的都市区不同，价格差异巨大。我想说的是，你可以预期其中一些库存位在几千美元的低端，比你想象的要低得多。

turns.speaker: Lenny
turns.en: For one billboard.
turns.zh: 一块广告牌。

turns.speaker: Zoelle Egner
turns.en: Yeah. So you don't need to get a million. And I'm not suggesting you go get one on 101. Good luck to you on that. That's expensive. But you can get one in a reasonable neighborhood in New York for way less money than you might expect, if you're willing to do remnant.
turns.zh: 对。所以你不需要花一百万。我也不是建议你去 101 公路上搞一块。祝你好运，那很贵。但如果你愿意拿剩余库存，你在纽约一个还算像样的社区搞一块，花的钱会比你预期的少得多。
